definition: In computer vision a camera matrix or (camera) projection matrix is a 3 × 4 {\displaystyle 3\times 4} matrix which describes the mapping of a pinhole camera from 3D points in the world to 2D points in an image.
details: Let x {\displaystyle \mathbf {x} } be a representation of a 3D point in homogeneous coordinates (a 4-dimensional vector), and let y {\displaystyle \mathbf {y} } be a representation of the image of this point in the pinhole camera (a 3-dimensional vector). Then the following relation holds y ∼ C x {\displaystyle \mathbf {y} \sim \mathbf {C} \,\mathbf {x} } where C {\displaystyle \mathbf {C} } is the camera matrix and the ∼ {\displaystyle \,\sim } sign implies that the left and right hand sides are equal except for a multiplication by a non-zero scalar k ≠ 0 {\displaystyle k\neq 0} : y = k C x . {\displaystyle \mathbf {y} =k\,\mathbf {C} \,\mathbf {x} .} Since the camera matrix C {\displaystyle \mathbf {C} } is involved in the mapping between elements of two projective spaces, it too can be regarded as a projective element. This means that it has only 11 degrees of freedom since any multiplication by a non-zero scalar results in an equivalent camera matrix.

explainer.lead: A camera matrix is a compact mathematical link between a 3D scene and a 2D image. For a pinhole camera, it lets computer-vision systems calculate where a world point appears in the image.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a simple camera turning the position of a toy into a dot on a photo. A camera matrix is like the instruction sheet for that conversion: you give it the toy's location, and it helps work out where the dot belongs.
tiers.practitioner: Represent the world point as a homogeneous 4-vector, multiply it by the 3 × 4 matrix, and interpret the resulting homogeneous 3-vector up to a non-zero scale before obtaining its 2D image position. Do not treat all 12 matrix entries as independent: multiplying the entire matrix by a non-zero scalar gives an equivalent projection, leaving 11 degrees of freedom.
tiers.paperLevel: For a pinhole camera, C is a 3 × 4 projection matrix such that y = k C x, where x is a homogeneous 4-vector, y is a homogeneous image 3-vector, and k is non-zero. C is itself projective: C and aC are equivalent for any non-zero scalar a, so C has 11 degrees of freedom.

explainer.example: Take C with rows [1,0,0,0], [0,1,0,0], and [0,0,1,0], and let x = (2,3,4,1). Then Cx = (2,3,4); after homogeneous normalization this is (1/2,3/4,1), so the corresponding 2D image point is (0.5,0.75).

usedIn.name: Computer vision
usedIn.detail: Represents the projection of 3D world points into 2D image points.

usedIn.name: Pinhole camera models
usedIn.detail: Provides the 3 × 4 matrix describing the camera's projective mapping.

explainer.intuition: Think of the matrix as packaging the pinhole camera's projection rule into one multiplication. It maps a point's homogeneous world coordinates to homogeneous image coordinates, with overall scale carrying no additional meaning.
howItWorks: Write the 3D world point as a homogeneous 4-vector x.
Multiply x by the 3 × 4 camera matrix C.
Read Cx as a homogeneous image vector, defined up to a non-zero scalar.
Normalize that image vector to obtain its 2D image position.
explainer.whyItMatters: It expresses the central 3D-to-2D mapping of a pinhole camera in a single compact object. Its projective interpretation also explains why scale is ambiguous and why the matrix has 11 rather than 12 degrees of freedom.
misconceptions: A 3 × 4 camera matrix has 12 independent degrees of freedom; it has 11 because overall scale is irrelevant.
Cx is already an ordinary 2D pixel coordinate; it is a homogeneous 3-vector defined up to scale.
Changing every entry of C by the same non-zero factor changes the projection; it produces an equivalent matrix.

diagram.caption: The camera matrix maps homogeneous world coordinates to homogeneous image coordinates, which are then normalized to a 2D point.
